Notice that our solid can be written as the type II region

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,\,0\le x\le 2+y-z\},
$$

where

$$
D=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 3,\,\,0\le z\le 2\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane, shown below.

![](images/59/59b7304dcc07ac38c093b7d8d29d4b4079f192cd9fd0385db9f1981e4640eceb.png)

Hence, the type II representation of $R$ is

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 3,\,\,0\le z\le 2,\,\,0\le x\le 2+y-z\}.
$$

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2+y-z}dx\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}[x]_{x=0}^{x=2+y-z}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}(2+y-z)-0\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}2+y-z\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{[(2+y)z-\frac{{z}^{2}}{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=2}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}((2+y)(2)-\frac{{2}^{2}}{2})-0\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}2+2y\,dy \\  & =[2y+{y}^{2}]_{y=0}^{y=3} \\  & =(2(3)+{3}^{2})-0 \\  & =15.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186128053 :answer-field/correct 17592186128058 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129763 :question/problem "Find the volume of the solid $R$ given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le \pi ,\,-2\le y\le 2,\,0\le z\le \operatorname{sin}⁡x\}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that we have a three-dimensional type I region.

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{-2}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,dz\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{-2}^{2}[z]_{z=0}^{z=\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{-2}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-0\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{-2}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡x[y]_{y=-2}^{y=2}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,(2-(-2))\,dx \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,dx \\  & =-4[\operatorname{cos}⁡x]_{x=0}^{x=\pi } \\  & =-4(-1-1) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186128059 :answer-field/correct 17592186128063 :answer-field/choices ["answer-4e0627ca-90a4-5c2d-835c-b255053c8381" "answer-e249f9ca-86be-5b5a-b69e-663670da563c"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4e0627ca-90a4-5c2d-835c-b255053c8381" :answer/id #uuid "4e0627ca-90a4-5c2d-835c-b255053c8381" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e249f9ca-86be-5b5a-b69e-663670da563c" :answer/id #uuid "e249f9ca-86be-5b5a-b69e-663670da563c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-8fb4dc8a-610a-5632-95eb-19ebf2c9f8b3" :question/id #uuid "8fb4dc8a-610a-5632-95eb-19ebf2c9f8b3" :question/math-academy-id "q-161697" :question/problem "![](images/a0/a0ad9cb5ea68b0018680d57d86d88a8dfcf7581a238e9368f566b2396f119579.png)

Find the volume of the solid region above.

*Hint: All surfaces, except for the right one, are parallel to the corresponding coordinate planes.*" :question/worked-solution "![](images/d7/d72b3c8aac80a46894d2b7c0c4956ced9eb5b4ebd663b73ba86096550e993bb8.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type III region

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,0\le y\le 3+\frac{x}{3}-z\},
$$

where

$$
D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 3,\,\,0\le z\le 2\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $xz$-plane, shown below.

![](images/a2/a2dbcefff1b7c28156f117b012c522dd65bca1c1ddd9e2bac4bf2e6ea1ce3722.png)

Hence, the type III representation of $R$ is

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 3,\,\,0\le z\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le 3+\frac{x}{3}-z\}
$$

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3+x/3-z}dy\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}[y]_{y=0}^{y=3+x/3-z}\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}(3+\frac{x}{3}-z)-0\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}3+\frac{x}{3}-z\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{[(3+\frac{x}{3})z-\frac{{z}^{2}}{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=2}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}((3+\frac{x}{3})(2)-\frac{{2}^{2}}{2})-0\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}4+\frac{2x}{3}\,dx \\  & ={[4x+\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=3} \\  & =(12+3)-0 \\  & =15.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-678a936d-2d59-5cda-bb5b-7ba53ed50f15"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id #uuid "6fae9a19-909c-5d4f-9c8f-4d34e1cb3eba" :question/math-academy-id "q-161713" :question/problem "Consider the solid enclosed between the paraboloid $x={y}^{2}+2{z}^{2}$ and the parabolic cylinder $x=3-2{y}^{2},$ whose volume can be written in terms of double integrals, as follows:

$$
V={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{a(y)}^{b(y)}\,f(y,z)\,dz\,dy
$$

What is ${a}^{2}+{b}^{2}+f?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to determine the projection of the intersection of our surfaces onto the $yz$-plane. So, let's find where they intersect.

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2} & =3-2{y}^{2} \\ 3{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

So, the projection of the intersection in the $yz$-plane is an ellipse.

Notice that our solid can be written as a type II region: 

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,\,{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2}\le x\le 3-2{y}^{2}\},
$$

where $D$ is the interior of the ellipse $3{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2}=3.$ 

As a result, the volume of $R$ is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2}}^{3-2{y}^{2}}\text{d}x]\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3-2{y}^{2})-({y}^{2}+2{z}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3-3{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the boundary of $D$ consists of 

- the lower part $z=-\sqrt{\frac{3(1-{y}^{2})}{2}},$ and

- the upper part $z=\sqrt{\frac{3(1-{y}^{2})}{2}},$

for $-1\le y\le 1.$ 

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}3-3{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-\sqrt{3(1-{y}^{2})/2}}^{\sqrt{3(1-{y}^{2})/2}}\,3-3{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}\,dz\,dy.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}+f & ={(-\sqrt{\frac{3(1-{y}^{2})}{2}})}^{2}+{(\sqrt{\frac{3(1-{y}^{2})}{2}})}^{2}+(3-3{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{3(1-{y}^{2})}{2}+\frac{3(1-{y}^{2})}{2}+(3-3{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}) \\  & =6-6{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b0c34a23-22e6-559b-8ba1-968780133734"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2} & =3-2{y}^{2} \\ 3{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

So, the projection of the intersection in the $yz$-plane is an ellipse.

Notice that our solid can be written as a type II region: 

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,\,{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2}\le x\le 3-2{y}^{2}\},
$$

where $D$ is the interior of the ellipse $3{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2}=3.$

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2}}^{3-2{y}^{2}}\text{d}x]\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3-2{y}^{2})-({y}^{2}+2{z}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3-3{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the boundary of $D$ consists of

$$

$$
V={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{a(y)}^{b(y)}\,f(y,z)\,dz\,dy
$$

What is ${a}^{2}+{b}^{2}+f?$"] ["question-6fae9a19-909c-5d4f-9c8f-4d34e1cb3eba" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to determine the projection of the intersection of our surfaces onto the $yz$-plane. So, let's find where they intersect.

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2} & =3-2{y}^{2} \\ 3{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

So, the projection of the intersection in the $yz$-plane is an ellipse.

Notice that our solid can be written as a type II region: 

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,\,{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2}\le x\le 3-2{y}^{2}\},
$$

where $D$ is the interior of the ellipse $3{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2}=3.$ 

As a result, the volume of $R$ is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2}}^{3-2{y}^{2}}\text{d}x]\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3-2{y}^{2})-({y}^{2}+2{z}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3-3{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the boundary of $D$ consists of 

- the lower part $z=-\sqrt{\frac{3(1-{y}^{2})}{2}},$ and

- the upper part $z=\sqrt{\frac{3(1-{y}^{2})}{2}},$

for $-1\le y\le 1.$ 

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}3-3{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-\sqrt{3(1-{y}^{2})/2}}^{\sqrt{3(1-{y}^{2})/2}}\,3-3{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}\,dz\,dy.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}+f & ={(-\sqrt{\frac{3(1-{y}^{2})}{2}})}^{2}+{(\sqrt{\frac{3(1-{y}^{2})}{2}})}^{2}+(3-3{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{3(1-{y}^{2})}{2}+\frac{3(1-{y}^{2})}{2}+(3-3{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}) \\  & =6-6{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-6fae9a19-909c-5d4f-9c8f-4d34e1cb3eba" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-b0c34a23-22e6-559b-8ba1-968780133734" :answer-field/id #uuid
